notes.h: Analysing the fitness demands of an activity
notes.b: Before you can say which fitness components matter, you need to break an activity down. This is the first step in applying the fitness components to a real sport, position or role.
points: Needs analysis means working out which fitness components an activity, position or role demands, by examining its duration, intensity, pattern of work and rest, the movements involved and the energy systems used (the ways the body produces energy for the muscles).
The performer's current fitness is then compared with those demands, usually by fitness testing, to find the gaps to train. This comparison is what turns the analysis into a training plan.
To examine the extent to which a component matters, rank it as essential, important or less important for the activity. Then justify each ranking with a specific moment of play or performance.

Positions and roles differ within one activity, so analyse the role, not just the sport. A soccer goalkeeper needs reaction time, power and agility more than cardio-respiratory endurance (the ability of the heart and lungs to keep supplying oxygen over long periods), while a midfielder needs the reverse.
notes.tip: When asked to discuss the extent to which a component is required, give a ranking and justify it with a specific moment from the activity, not just a definition. Name the role as well when it matters.

notes.h: Fitness profile: an invasion game (Gaelic football)
notes.b: An invasion game is one where two teams move into each other's territory to score. Gaelic football mixes long running with sudden bursts, so it draws on many components at once.
points: Cardio-respiratory endurance (essential): players cover long distances over two halves and must recover between efforts, so a strong heart and lungs keep supplying oxygen to the working muscles.
Speed (essential): the ability to move the body quickly, needed to win the race to a breaking ball or to get away from a marker (the opponent guarding you).
Agility (essential): the ability to change direction quickly while keeping control, needed to side-step a tackler or turn quickly in defence.
Power (important): the ability to produce force quickly, a mix of strength and speed. It is needed to jump for a high catch and to kick long.
Muscular endurance (important): the ability of a muscle to keep working without tiring. The legs must keep going for repeated sprints and challenges late in the game.
notes.tip: For a game like this, give each component a rank and tie it to a moment of play, such as the sprint to a breaking ball or the jump for a catch. Examiners want the reason, not just a list of components.

notes.h: Fitness profile: an aesthetic activity (artistic gymnastics)
notes.b: An aesthetic activity is judged on how the movement looks as well as what is achieved. Artistic gymnastics is made of short, controlled routines, so the profile is very different from a running game.
points: Flexibility (essential): the range of movement at a joint, needed for splits, walkovers and extended body lines, which are marked on how they look.
Strength (essential): the most force a muscle can produce, needed to support body weight in balances and on the hands.
Balance (essential): the ability to keep the body steady, needed for held positions and landings, where a wobble or step costs control.
Power (essential): force produced quickly, needed for the explosive jumps, tumbles and vaults.
Co-ordination (essential): using the senses and body parts together smoothly, needed to link elements of a routine fluently.
Cardio-respiratory endurance (less important): routines are short, so the heart and lungs are not pushed for long periods.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to pick the main components for an activity and explain. Gymnastics is a good contrast to a team game, because cardio-respiratory endurance is less important while flexibility, strength, balance, power and co-ordination are essential.

notes.h: Fitness profile: an endurance activity (distance running)
notes.b: In an endurance activity the performer keeps going at a steady pace for a long time. The profile is narrow: a few components matter very much and most others matter little.
points: Cardio-respiratory endurance (essential): the event lasts many minutes or hours at a steady pace, so the heart and lungs must keep delivering oxygen to the muscles throughout.
Muscular endurance (essential): the legs repeat thousands of strides, so the leg muscles must resist fatigue (tiring) over the whole race.

Body composition (important): the proportion of the body that is fat compared with muscle and bone. A low body-fat percentage reduces the weight carried, so the runner uses less energy at each stride.
Reaction time (less important): the time taken to respond to a signal. A slow start matters little over a long race, because a fraction of a second is tiny compared with the whole event.
notes.tip: You may be asked to name the main component for two contrasting events, such as 10,000 m and shot-put, and explain. For the long event, cardio-respiratory endurance is the main one, and your explanation should say why.

notes.h: Developing fitness in a demanding practice context
notes.b: Fitness can be trained inside the activity itself, while skills are practised under the fatigue and pressure of competition. This is what a demanding practice context means.
points: Methods include conditioned games (games with extra rules that force a type of work), small-sided games (fewer players on a smaller pitch), game-speed drills and skill circuits.
Example: a small-sided possession game with a two-touch limit develops cardio-respiratory endurance, agility and speed while players pass and move.
Example: a dribbling relay through cones develops speed, agility and co-ordination.
Benefit: specificity, because players use the same movements, energy systems and decisions as in competition, so the fitness gained transfers directly to the match.
Benefit: it is motivating and time-efficient, because fitness and skill are trained together, and it trains skill execution under fatigue.
Limitation: intensity and overload (working harder than the body is used to) are harder to control precisely, and some players work less than others.
Limitation: it may not develop maximal strength or flexibility, so it is combined with training outside the activity. There is more on this in Designing a fitness plan.
notes.tip: When asked how fitness can be developed in practice, give a named method, an example with the components it trains, a benefit and a limitation. Specificity is the key benefit to name.

notes.h: A combined approach to health- and performance-related fitness
notes.b: Health-related fitness (HRF) components support general health, while performance-related fitness (PRF) components support success in a sport. A combined approach trains one of each together, which saves time and links the training to the activity.
points: A combined approach develops a health-related and a performance-related component in the same activity or session. It must name one HRF and one PRF component and train both together.

To design one, name the two components, describe what the performer does with sets, repetitions or time, and state how it progresses. Then explain how each component is trained and link it to the activity's demands.

Example, flexibility (HRF) and balance (PRF): a single-leg balance-and-reach routine, standing on one leg and reaching the free foot out slowly to points around the body through a full range. It progresses to an unstable surface, which makes balance harder.
Example, muscular endurance (HRF) and agility (PRF): a circuit alternating ladder footwork drills with body-weight squats and lunges, with timed work and rest at each station.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to choose one HRF and one PRF component and outline one activity that trains both. Name both components, describe the work with sets, repetitions or time, and say how it progresses and links to the activity.

keyTerms.definition: Working out which fitness components an activity or role demands from its duration, intensity, work-to-rest pattern, movements and energy systems.
A game with modified rules, such as limited touches or a smaller area, used to develop particular skills or fitness.
A game with fewer players and a smaller area, which increases involvement and intensity.
Training a health-related and a performance-related fitness component together in one activity or session.

factCards.term: Combined approach example: flexibility and balance
factCards.definition: A single-leg balance-and-reach routine through a full range of movement, progressing to an unstable surface.

factCards.term: Main fitness component: 10,000 m runner and shot-putter
factCards.definition: 10,000 m: cardio-respiratory endurance, for a long, steady aerobic effort. Shot-put: power, for an explosive throw.

factCards.term: Two benefits and one limitation of training fitness inside the activity
factCards.definition: Benefits: specificity; motivating and trains skill under fatigue. Limitation: overload is hard to control.

questions.prompt: Discuss the extent to which reaction time, muscular endurance and power are required in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Activity: basketball. Power is essential: players jump for rebounds and blocks and push off explosively to drive past a defender, so strength applied at speed decides who wins the ball. Reaction time is important: defenders react to a dribbler's change of direction and to deflected passes, and players react to loose balls, but anticipation and reading the play reduce how much depends on raw reaction. Muscular endurance is important: the legs must keep a low defensive stance and repeat jumps over four quarters, and when it fails, shooting and defending suffer late in the game. Overall, power is the most decisive of the three, but all three are needed.

questions.prompt: Outline one activity that could be used as a combined approach to training flexibility and balance in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Activity: soccer. A single-leg balance-and-reach routine: the player stands on one leg with a slight bend at the knee and slowly reaches the free foot as far as possible forward, sideways and backward, touching the floor lightly each time, for three sets of five reaches on each leg. Reaching to the end of the range at the hip develops flexibility (health-related), while holding the body steady over one foot develops dynamic balance (performance-related). It progresses by standing on a cushion or wobble board. Both are needed in soccer for stretching to reach a ball and staying balanced while striking it.

questions.prompt: Identify the main component of fitness needed by a marathon runner and by a shot-putter and explain each choice.
questions.model: Marathon runner: cardio-respiratory endurance, because the race lasts over two hours at a steady pace and depends on a continuous supply of oxygen to the muscles. Shot-putter: power, because the throw is a single explosive effort lasting a few seconds in which strength must be applied at high speed.
